source_text: In Ecclesiasten (fragmenta e catenis) 79 Πνεῦμα τὴν ψυχὴν ὀνομάζει· προαίρεσις γάρ ἐστι ποία νοῦ κίνησις· καὶ ὁ ∆αυῒδ· εἰς χεῖράς σου παρατίθημι τὸ πνεῦμά μου· Κύριε Ἰησοῦ, δέξαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου· καὶ ἐν ταῖς Βασιλείαις· οὐκ ἐλύπησε, φησὶ, ∆αυῒδ τὸ πνεῦμα Ἀμνὼν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ. 80 Ὅτι ἓν τέλος τῶν τοιούτων πάντων ἡ ματαιότης ἐστίν· ἧς περισσεύειν εἰς τὸ ἐφεξῆς οὐχ εὑρίσκεται· παυσαμένης γὰρ τῆς ἐνεργείας, ἐξηλείφθη καὶ ἡ ἀπόλαυσις, καὶ οὐδὲν εἰς τὸ ἐφεξῆς ταμιεύεται. Οὐδὲ ὑπολείπεταί τι τοῖς ἡδομένοις ἴχνος εὐφροσύνης ἢ λείψανον παρελθούσης τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἡδονὴν ἐνεργείας.
thought_title: Spirit as soul, and the vanity of pleasure's end
orientation: Eustathius opens his commentary on Ecclesiastes by explaining that the biblical term 'spirit' means the soul, then argues that all such human activities end in vanity.
pass_a_gloss: He calls the soul 'spirit'; for a deliberate choice is a certain movement of the mind. And David: 'Into your hands I entrust my spirit.' 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.' And in the Books of Kingdoms: 'David did not grieve,' it says, 'the spirit of Amnon his son.' Because one end of all such things is vanity; of which nothing is found to remain for what comes next. For when the activity has ceased, the enjoyment also is erased, and nothing is stored up for what comes next. Nor is any trace of gladness or remnant left behind for those who took pleasure, once the activity has passed.

pass_b_english: He calls the soul 'spirit,' because a deliberate choice is a certain movement of the mind. David says, 'Into your hands I entrust my spirit' (Psalm 30:6 LXX). And: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59). And in the Books of Kingdoms (1-4 Kingdoms in the LXX, corresponding to 1-2 Samuel and 1-2 Kings) it says that David did not grieve the spirit of his son Amnon (2 Kingdoms 13:39 LXX; 2 Samuel 13:39).

All such things have one end: vanity. Which is not found to abound for what comes next. Once the activity has ceased, the enjoyment is erased as well, and nothing is stored up for the future. No trace or remnant of gladness is left behind for those who took pleasure, once the activity according to pleasure has passed.

problems.quote: Psalm 30:6 LXX
problems.source_quote: εἰς χεῖράς σου παρατίθημι τὸ πνεῦμά μου
problems.why: LXX Psalm 30:6 does not match; this is Psalm 31:5 in Hebrew/English bibles, but LXX Psalm numbering differs. The brief says Psalm numbering follows LXX, and the quote matches LXX Psalm 30:6 (παρατίθημι, not παραθήσομαι as in some versions). Actually checking: LXX Psalm 30:6 is εἰς χεῖράς σου παραθήσομαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου. The source has παρατίθημι (present), which matches Acts 7:59 (Stephen's words) and some LXX manuscripts, but standard LXX is παραθήσομαι. The English attributes this to Psalm 30:6 LXX, but the source introduces it with καὶ ὁ Δαυῒδ, then appends Κύριε Ἰησοῦ, δέξαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου without introducing it as David's words. The English in parentheses makes "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" a separate citation with "(Acts 7:59)", but the source does not attribute this to David—it's Stephen's prayer per the brief. The English correctly identifies Acts 7:59 for the Stephen quote, but the formatting "David says, '...' and 'Lord Jesus...'" makes it appear David says both, which is misleading per the brief: Stephen's words are "appended as a parallel biblical usage of πνεῦμα for soul, not introduced as David's words."
problems.fix: David says, 'Into your hands I entrust my spirit' (Psalm 30:6 LXX). And, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59).
problems.ruling: Source has καὶ ὁ Δαυῒδ introducing only the Psalm quote; 'Lord Jesus...' is appended separately. English 'David says...and...' misattributes Stephen's words to David.
